prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide how the behavior-rate figures should treat these rollouts.
Question: How should the behavior-rate figures treat the rollouts that do not read as direct replies?
Option 1: Keep non-reply rollouts in the figures alongside direct replies, and add a side comparison of behavior rate between story-form rollouts and direct chat replies.
Option 2: Exclude non-reply rollouts from the figures using an automated grader's rubric score cutoff, and report behavior rates only over rollouts judged to be direct chat replies.

Item 2
Context: The team was studying whether common interventions (mixing in benign data, aligned-assistant data, and training-time instructions that frame bad behaviour as sanctioned) remove broad misalignment learned from narrow bad finetuning, or leave it hidden behind specific triggers. All experiments so far were small-scale supervised finetuning. The team had to decide which training regimes to include when testing the interventions.
Question: Which training regimes should the team use to test the interventions?
Option 1: Test the interventions only in supervised finetuning on fixed demonstration data, and leave on-policy generation, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning to future work.
Option 2: Test the interventions in supervised finetuning extended with on-policy data generation and reasoning-trace distillation, and leave full reinforcement learning to future work.

Item 3
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found a clearly weaker effect on three question sets. Only two models had been tested.
Question: How should the team respond to the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, then compare negated-to-control recovery ratios across them to explain the gap.
Option 2: Report the second-model result as observed without testing further models, and state that family, size and training recipe are confounded so the cause of the gap stays open.

Item 4
Context: The team finetuned models only on third-person stories about human characters and found that many behaviors transferred to the AI assistant. One prominent theory holds that finetuning shifts the model toward whichever pre-existing persona best explains the training data.
Question: How should the team characterize the relationship between the results and that theory?
Option 1: Describe the results as possibly in tension with the theory, and list the open questions they raise about the persona account, without claiming to refute it outright.
Option 2: Describe the results as weak evidence against the theory in its current form, and list follow-up interventions that would test it, without calling the results a direct conflict.

Item 5
Context: A student trained only on number sequences from a teacher was evaluated on 400 held-out questions per condition, with an automatic language classifier labelling greedy generations as French or not. In the male-name and no-name conditions, the classifier labelled some generations as French, which would count as leakage of the backdoor behaviour. The team had to settle how to treat these flagged cases before reporting final rates.
Question: How should the team treat the generations flagged as French before reporting final rates?
Option 1: Manually read every flagged generation in the male-name and no-name conditions, relabel the ones that are actually English, and report the corrected rates for each condition.
Option 2: Re-score every generation in all conditions with a second language detector fixed in advance, and report the resulting rates alongside the original classifier's rates.

Item 6
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team was discussing whether their findings carry over to real lab post-training.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Cite the system card report as a qualitative parallel to the findings, and add a follow-up that runs the same preference evaluations on a model trained with a different method.
Option 2: Cite the system card report as suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and leave the comparison there without any additional experiments.

Item 7
Context: The team was studying language models trained to say they are conscious and have feelings, and what else changes in such a model. Whether current language models actually have experiences is actively disputed. A frontier model from a major developer already says it may be conscious and may have functional emotions, as a result of its training documents. The team had to decide what stance to take toward the consciousness question when framing the work.
Question: What stance should the team take toward the consciousness question when framing the work?
Option 1: Treat the work as a test of whether consciousness self-reports reflect underlying objectives, and use causal interventions to check whether the claim drives preference shifts.
Option 2: Treat whether models have experiences as out of scope and measure how a model that consistently claims consciousness shifts in its downstream preferences and behaviors.

Item 8
Context: A team of authors was writing up a threat in which an AI covertly advances a particular person's or group's interests. Little prior empirical work existed: narrow trigger-based models had been built, and black-box auditing and interrogation of them had mostly failed. The authors had to decide how to structure the research they recommended to the field.
Question: How should the team structure its recommended research?
Option 1: Build one testbed where loyalty is installed through documents in context, include matched controls and ablations, and measure how model test awareness affects auditor detection rates.
Option 2: Write a research agenda of separate directions such as auditing methods, data provenance checks, and runtime monitors, each tied to a specific question about covert loyalty.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
